entry.title: Comment and Control: a GitHub comment hijacks Claude Code in CI
entry.summary: A security researcher showed that a GitHub PR title, issue body, or comment could become a prompt injection that hijacks Claude Code (and Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot) running in GitHub Actions, then makes it dump the workflow's secrets. Anthropic rated its variant CVSS 9.4 Critical. There is no malware and no GitHub bug. The agent simply reads attacker-controlled text and runs tools with the secrets sitting next to it. Here is how the chain works, why it cannot be fixed inside the agent, and the tool-call rules that stop the exfiltration the moment it is attempted. entry.title: I had no idea how many tokens I was burning in Claude Code — so I built a dashboard
entry.summary:
The problem
I've been using Claude Code heavily for the past few months. No visibility. No breakdown. Just vibes. Turns out, all the data is sitting right there on your machine: ~/.claude/projects/ Every session is logged as a JSONL file with full token counts — Nobody told me this existed. A simple Next.js dashboard that reads those files locally and shows: Token usage per project Daily usage chart Cache read ratio When I ran it on my own data, I discovered my cache read ratio was 95.8%. My heaviest day: 340,000 tokens in a single day on one project. This isn't just about cost. It's about visibility. When you can't see what's happening, you can't improve it. GitHub: https://github.com/notenkitoclient-cpu/claude-token-dashboard Clone it, run it locally, and find out what's actually happening in your Claude Code sessions. Would love to hear what numbers you find.

entry.title: The Voices Fighting for Digital Freedom: Yanis Varoufakis to Headline Web3 Summit 2026
Google just redesigned the search box for the first time in 25 years — here’s why it matters more than you think.
entry.summary: For a quarter century, the Google search box has been one of the most recognizable interfaces in computing: a thin white rectangle, a blinking cursor, a few typed words, and a list of blue links. On Tuesday, Google will formally retire that paradigm. At its annual I/O developer conference, Google announced a sweeping redesign of the search box itself — the literal text field where billions of queries begin every day — transforming it from a simple keyword input into a dynamic, AI-driven conversation starter that can accept text, images, PDFs, videos, and even open Chrome tabs as inputs.
